Aliases/Keywords: itching, itchy, scratchy skin, skin irritation
Common Causes: Dry skin, mild allergic reaction, insect bites, sweating, rough fabric, stress
Natural/Home Remedies: Cool, wet compress or ice pack on the itchy area for 10-20 minutes; colloidal oatmeal bath soak; fragrance-free moisturizer applied right after bathing; diluted peppermint or menthol lotion
Self-Care Tips: Keep nails short to limit scratching damage; avoid very hot showers; use a humidifier in dry weather; switch to fragrance-free soap and detergent
When to See a Doctor: Itching lasts more than 2 weeks, spreads widely, or comes with rash, swelling, yellow crusting, or fever

Aliases/Keywords: dry skin, flaky skin, rough skin, ashy skin
Common Causes: Cold or low-humidity weather, long hot showers, harsh soaps, frequent hand-washing, ageing
Natural/Home Remedies: Apply a thick, fragrance-free moisturizer (e.g. petroleum jelly or a heavy cream) within a few minutes of bathing while skin is still damp; coconut oil on very dry patches
Self-Care Tips: Limit showers/baths to 5-10 minutes with warm (not hot) water; use a gentle, non-foaming cleanser; run a humidifier indoors; pat skin dry instead of rubbing
When to See a Doctor: Skin is inflamed, painful, cracked with bleeding, or doesn't improve after a couple of weeks of consistent moisturizing

Aliases/Keywords: oily face, shiny skin, greasy skin
Common Causes: Overactive sebaceous (oil) glands, hormones, heat/humidity, over-washing which triggers rebound oil
Natural/Home Remedies: Blotting papers for quick shine control; a light, oil-free gel moisturizer instead of skipping moisturizer entirely
Self-Care Tips: Wash face twice a day with a gentle, oil-free cleanser (avoid over-washing); choose noncomedogenic, oil-free makeup and sunscreen; avoid touching your face often
When to See a Doctor: Oiliness is accompanied by painful cystic breakouts or sudden, unexplained change in oil production

Aliases/Keywords: oily T-zone, dry cheeks, combination skin type
Common Causes: Genetics; oil glands are more active on the forehead/nose/chin than on the cheeks
Natural/Home Remedies: Use a lightweight moisturizer on oily areas and a richer one on drier areas
Self-Care Tips: A gentle, balanced cleanser used on the whole face; avoid products marketed only for 'oily' or only for 'dry' skin, which can overtreat one zone
When to See a Doctor: Persistent redness, stinging, or breakouts that don't respond to a simplified routine

Aliases/Keywords: skin sensitivity, stinging, burning after product use, reactive skin
Common Causes: A weakened skin barrier, frequent product changes, over-exfoliation, fragrance or alcohol in products
Natural/Home Remedies: Simplify to a short routine: gentle cleanser, fragrance-free moisturizer, mineral sunscreen
Self-Care Tips: Patch-test new products on the inner forearm for a few days before using on the face; avoid layering many active ingredients at once; reintroduce products one at a time
When to See a Doctor: Persistent burning, swelling, or a rash that develops after a specific product

Aliases/Keywords: sunburn, burnt skin, red skin from sun
Common Causes: Excess ultraviolet (UV) exposure from sunlight (can happen even on cloudy days)
Natural/Home Remedies: Cool bath or shower, or a cool damp cloth on the skin; a fragrance-free aftersun lotion or gel containing aloe vera; extra water to counter dehydration
Self-Care Tips: Avoid direct sun until skin heals; do not pop blisters or peel skin; avoid petroleum jelly and ice directly on burnt skin; loose, soft clothing over the area
When to See a Doctor: Blistering over a large area, fever, chills, dizziness, nausea, or sunburn on a young child or baby

Aliases/Keywords: prickly heat, sweat rash, heat bumps
Common Causes: Sweat trapped under the skin in hot, humid weather or from tight clothing
Natural/Home Remedies: Cool showers; a cool, damp cloth held on the rash; gentle exfoliation to help unclog sweat ducts once the rash has settled
Self-Care Tips: Move to a cooler, air-conditioned space; wear loose, breathable cotton clothing; keep the area dry and uncovered; avoid heavy, greasy creams that trap moisture
When to See a Doctor: The area becomes painful, swollen, warm, or starts oozing pus, which can suggest infection

Aliases/Keywords: chafed skin folds, rash under breasts/armpits/groin, friction rash
Common Causes: Sweat and friction trapped in skin folds (underarms, groin, under breasts, between rolls)
Natural/Home Remedies: Keep the area cool and dry; a cotton cloth or dusting powder can absorb moisture between folds
Self-Care Tips: Wear breathable fabrics; dry skin folds thoroughly after washing; avoid tight clothing that traps moisture
When to See a Doctor: The area looks white/soggy, smells unusual, or is very painful, which can point to a yeast or bacterial infection needing treatment

Aliases/Keywords: mosquito bite, bug bite, bee sting, itchy bite
Common Causes: Mosquitoes, fleas, other biting or stinging insects
Natural/Home Remedies: Wash the area with cool water and mild soap; a cold compress or ice wrapped in cloth to numb the itch; calamine lotion for itching
Self-Care Tips: Avoid scratching, which can break the skin and cause infection; remove a visible stinger by scraping (not squeezing) it out
When to See a Doctor: Signs of spreading infection (increasing redness, warmth, pus), a very large local reaction, or any difficulty breathing/swelling of the face or throat (seek emergency care immediately)

Aliases/Keywords: contact rash, allergic rash, reaction to soap/detergent, skin reacting to product
Common Causes: Skin reacting to a soap, detergent, fragrance, new skincare product, jewelry (nickel), or plant contact
Natural/Home Remedies: Stop using the suspected product immediately; a cool compress and fragrance-free moisturizer to calm irritation; a light coating of colloidal oatmeal lotion
Self-Care Tips: Identify and avoid the trigger; switch to fragrance-free, hypoallergenic products; wash the area gently with mild soap and water as soon as possible after contact
When to See a Doctor: The rash is widespread, affects the face, eyes, mouth, or genitals, or doesn't settle within a few days

Aliases/Keywords: dry lips, chapped lips, cracked lip corners
Common Causes: Cold/dry/windy weather, licking lips frequently, dehydration, breathing through the mouth
Natural/Home Remedies: A plain, fragrance-free lip balm reapplied often; a thin layer of petroleum jelly at night; staying well hydrated
Self-Care Tips: Avoid licking lips (saliva makes dryness worse); use a humidifier in dry indoor air; protect lips from wind and sun with an SPF lip balm
When to See a Doctor: Peeling or cracking doesn't improve after consistent care, or the corners of the mouth are persistently sore/cracked (can suggest a nutrient deficiency or infection)

Aliases/Keywords: dry heels, heel fissures, cracked feet
Common Causes: Prolonged standing, dry skin, open-backed shoes, thickened callused skin
Natural/Home Remedies: Soak feet in warm water for 10 minutes, then gently smooth thickened skin with a pumice stone; apply a thick foot cream or petroleum jelly and wear socks overnight
Self-Care Tips: Moisturize feet daily, especially after bathing; avoid walking barefoot on hard, dry surfaces; choose well-fitted, closed-back shoes
When to See a Doctor: Cracks are deep, bleeding, or painful to walk on, especially if you have diabetes or poor circulation

Aliases/Keywords: rough bumps on arms, chicken skin, KP, goosebump skin
Common Causes: A buildup of keratin (skin protein) blocking hair follicles; genetics; tends to worsen with dry skin
Natural/Home Remedies: Regular moisturizing with a cream-based, fragrance-free moisturizer; gentle exfoliation 2-3 times a week (avoid harsh scrubbing)
Self-Care Tips: Avoid tight, rough fabrics like wool; keep showers short and lukewarm rather than hot; be patient — it often fades with age
When to See a Doctor: Bumps become very red, inflamed, or you want a professional opinion on treatment options

Aliases/Keywords: melasma, pregnancy mask, hormonal dark patches
Common Causes: Hormonal changes (pregnancy, birth control), sun exposure, genetics
Natural/Home Remedies: Consistent, generous use of a broad-spectrum sunscreen (tinted mineral sunscreens with iron oxide block visible light in addition to UV)
Self-Care Tips: Reapply sunscreen every two hours when outdoors; wear a wide-brimmed hat; avoid direct midday sun; be patient, as melasma can be slow to fade even with care
When to See a Doctor: Patches are cosmetically distressing or spreading — a dermatologist can discuss additional options; also mention any new patches to a doctor if pregnant

Aliases/Keywords: dark marks after pimples, acne scars discoloration, dark spots
Common Causes: Skin's healing response after acne, cuts, burns, or other injury/inflammation
Natural/Home Remedies: Daily sunscreen to prevent the spots from darkening further; gentle skincare that avoids re-irritating the healing skin
Self-Care Tips: Avoid picking at acne or scabs, which worsens dark marks; be patient, since these marks often fade over months on their own
When to See a Doctor: Marks are not fading after several months, or you want guidance on options to speed up fading

Aliases/Keywords: sunspots, age spots, liver spots, dark spots from sun
Common Causes: Cumulative sun exposure over the years
Natural/Home Remedies: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen to prevent new spots and stop existing ones from darkening
Self-Care Tips: Wear protective clothing and a hat outdoors; reapply sunscreen every two hours in the sun; check new or changing spots against a mole map periodically
When to See a Doctor: Any spot changes in size, shape, or color, becomes raised, bleeds, or doesn't heal — this needs prompt evaluation to rule out skin cancer

Aliases/Keywords: under eye circles, dark under eyes, tired-looking eyes
Common Causes: Lack of sleep, genetics, thinning skin with age, allergies, dehydration
Natural/Home Remedies: A cold compress (or chilled spoon/cucumber slices) held under the eyes for 5-10 minutes; cooled chamomile or green tea bags
Self-Care Tips: Prioritize consistent, adequate sleep; stay hydrated; elevate your head slightly while sleeping; manage seasonal allergies if they contribute
When to See a Doctor: Sudden dark circles with swelling, pain, or vision changes, which should be checked promptly

Aliases/Keywords: puffy eyes, eye bags, swollen eyelids
Common Causes: Fluid retention, lack of sleep, allergies, high salt intake, crying
Natural/Home Remedies: A cold compress or chilled spoons over closed eyes for a few minutes
Self-Care Tips: Sleep with your head slightly elevated; reduce salt intake; manage allergies if relevant
When to See a Doctor: Puffiness is sudden, one-sided, painful, or comes with redness or vision changes

Aliases/Keywords: pimples, breakouts, blackheads, whiteheads, clogged pores
Common Causes: Clogged pores from oil and dead skin cells, hormones, some cosmetics
Natural/Home Remedies: A gentle, oil-free cleanser used twice daily; oil-free, noncomedogenic moisturizer and makeup
Self-Care Tips: Never pick or pop pimples, which can worsen inflammation and scarring; wash pillowcases regularly; avoid heavy, pore-clogging products; remove makeup before bed
When to See a Doctor: Acne is painful, cystic, leaving scars, or not improving after weeks of a gentle, consistent routine

Aliases/Keywords: back acne, bacne, chest breakouts, body breakouts
Common Causes: Sweat and friction from tight clothing/gym gear, clogged pores, hormones
Natural/Home Remedies: Rinse off sweat promptly after exercise; a gentle, oil-free body wash
Self-Care Tips: Shower soon after sweating; wear loose, breathable, moisture-wicking fabric for workouts; avoid heavy oils/lotions on acne-prone areas
When to See a Doctor: Breakouts are widespread, painful, or leaving scars

Aliases/Keywords: razor burn, ingrown hair bumps, shaving irritation
Common Causes: Shaving against the grain, dull blades, dry shaving, tight-curling hair re-entering the skin
Natural/Home Remedies: A cool, damp cloth on freshly shaved skin; a fragrance-free, alcohol-free aftershave balm or aloe vera gel
Self-Care Tips: Shave with a sharp, clean blade in the direction of hair growth; soften skin with warm water and shaving cream first; avoid stretching skin taut while shaving
When to See a Doctor: Bumps become infected (increasing redness, pus, pain) or scarring develops

Aliases/Keywords: ingrown hair, hair bump, trapped hair
Common Causes: Hair curling back into the skin after shaving, waxing, or plucking, especially with curly hair
Natural/Home Remedies: Warm compress to soften skin and help the hair release; gentle exfoliation to clear dead skin over the follicle
Self-Care Tips: Avoid picking or digging out the hair with tweezers/needles at home, which risks infection and scarring; consider growing hair out for a period to reduce recurrence
When to See a Doctor: Signs of infection (redness, swelling, pus) or repeated ingrown hairs causing dark, raised scars

Aliases/Keywords: thigh chafing, skin rubbing rash, friction burn
Common Causes: Skin rubbing against skin or clothing repeatedly, often during exercise or in hot weather
Natural/Home Remedies: A cool compress on irritated skin; a fragrance-free healing balm once the skin is clean and dry
Self-Care Tips: Wear moisture-wicking, well-fitted clothing; apply an anti-chafe balm or powder to friction-prone areas before activity
When to See a Doctor: The area is broken, bleeding, or shows signs of infection

Aliases/Keywords: stretch marks, striae, skin stretching lines
Common Causes: Rapid skin stretching (growth spurts, pregnancy, weight change) that stretches the deeper skin layer
Natural/Home Remedies: Regular moisturizing with a rich cream may improve comfort and skin texture, though it won't fully prevent or erase marks
Self-Care Tips: Keep skin well hydrated during periods of rapid growth or weight change; be aware most fade in color over time on their own
When to See a Doctor: You want to discuss cosmetic options to reduce their appearance with a dermatologist

Aliases/Keywords: windburned skin, wind-chapped face, wind irritation
Common Causes: Cold, dry wind stripping the skin's natural moisture barrier, often on the face
Natural/Home Remedies: A thick, fragrance-free moisturizer or balm to repair the skin barrier; avoid hot water on the area, which worsens irritation
Self-Care Tips: Cover exposed skin with a scarf in windy, cold weather; apply a protective barrier balm before going outside; use sunscreen even in cold weather
When to See a Doctor: Skin is cracked, bleeding, or extremely painful

Aliases/Keywords: chilblains, cold sores on fingers/toes (non-viral), cold-damaged skin
Common Causes: Small blood vessels reacting abnormally to cold, then rapid rewarming, usually on fingers, toes, ears, or nose
Natural/Home Remedies: Warm the area gradually (not with direct heat like a hot water bottle, which can worsen symptoms); keep the area dry
Self-Care Tips: Dress warmly in layers, especially hands and feet, in cold weather; avoid rapid temperature changes; keep moving to maintain circulation
When to See a Doctor: Skin breaks open, becomes very painful, or shows signs of infection

Aliases/Keywords: dry hands, cracked knuckles, hand dermatitis from washing
Common Causes: Frequent hand-washing or sanitizer use, cold weather, harsh soap
Natural/Home Remedies: A thick hand cream or petroleum jelly applied right after washing; wearing cotton gloves over moisturized hands overnight
Self-Care Tips: Use a mild, fragrance-free soap; pat hands dry rather than rubbing; wear gloves for wet or cold-weather chores
When to See a Doctor: Cracks are deep, bleeding, or painful, or a rash spreads up the wrists

Aliases/Keywords: foot blister, friction blister, shoe blister
Common Causes: Repeated rubbing against skin, often from new or ill-fitting shoes
Natural/Home Remedies: Leave small, unbroken blisters intact to heal naturally; if a blister has already burst, gently clean with mild soap and water and cover loosely
Self-Care Tips: Cushion the area with a soft bandage or blister pad; break in new shoes gradually; wear moisture-wicking socks
When to See a Doctor: Signs of infection (increasing redness, warmth, pus, red streaking), or blisters from a burn/sunburn covering a large area

Aliases/Keywords: bruise, black and blue mark, minor bump bruise
Common Causes: Small blood vessels breaking under the skin after a bump or knock
Natural/Home Remedies: A cold compress or ice pack wrapped in cloth for the first 24-48 hours to reduce swelling; gentle elevation of the area
Self-Care Tips: Rest the area if possible; avoid pressing on the bruise; bruises typically fade through color changes over 1-2 weeks
When to See a Doctor: Bruising is severe, unexplained, doesn't fade, or is accompanied by significant swelling or pain suggesting a deeper injury

Issue: Peeling skin (after sun exposure or general)
Aliases/Keywords: skin peeling, flaking skin, shedding skin
Common Causes: Sunburn healing, very dry skin, over-exfoliation, harsh weather
Natural/Home Remedies: Keep the area gently moisturized with a fragrance-free lotion; avoid picking or peeling skin manually
Self-Care Tips: Let peeling skin shed naturally; avoid further sun exposure or harsh products until skin has recovered; use lukewarm (not hot) water
When to See a Doctor: Peeling covers a large area with pain, oozing, or fever, which needs medical attention

Aliases/Keywords: blotchy skin, uneven complexion, patchy skin color
Common Causes: Sun exposure, leftover marks from acne/injury, dehydration, inconsistent skincare
Natural/Home Remedies: Consistent, gentle skincare plus daily sunscreen tends to even tone out gradually over time
Self-Care Tips: Avoid harsh scrubbing or frequent product switching, which can trigger more irritation and unevenness; stay hydrated
When to See a Doctor: Patches are new, rapidly changing, or asymmetric — worth a dermatologist check

Aliases/Keywords: big pores, enlarged pores, visible pores
Common Causes: Genetics, oil production, sun damage reducing skin elasticity, aging
Natural/Home Remedies: A gentle exfoliating cleanse a couple of times a week to prevent pores from becoming clogged and appearing larger
Self-Care Tips: Keep skin clean and moisturized (skipping moisturizer can increase oil production); use noncomedogenic products; wear daily sunscreen to preserve skin elasticity
When to See a Doctor: Pores are associated with painful cystic acne, which needs a dermatologist's input

Aliases/Keywords: rough elbows, dry knees, flaky patches
Common Causes: Thicker skin in these areas combined with general dryness and less natural oil
Natural/Home Remedies: A thick balm or petroleum jelly-based moisturizer applied at night; gentle exfoliation with a soft cloth before moisturizing
Self-Care Tips: Moisturize these areas daily, not just when they feel dry; avoid harsh soaps directly on rough patches
When to See a Doctor: Patches become scaly, silvery, or don't respond to consistent moisturizing, which could suggest an underlying skin condition

Aliases/Keywords: milk spots, tiny white bumps, milia under eyes
Common Causes: Dead skin cells trapped just under the skin's surface, common around the eyes and cheeks
Natural/Home Remedies: Gentle exfoliation as part of a normal routine may help prevent buildup, but milia often resolve on their own over weeks to months
Self-Care Tips: Avoid squeezing or trying to extract them at home, which can cause scarring or infection; use noncomedogenic skincare
When to See a Doctor: Milia are widespread, persistent for months, or you'd like them professionally extracted

Aliases/Keywords: sweaty skin, body odor, underarm sweat
Common Causes: Heat, exercise, stress, hormonal changes, certain foods
Natural/Home Remedies: Wash sweat-prone areas daily with a gentle cleanser; a natural deodorant with baking soda or a mineral salt stone for mild odor control
Self-Care Tips: Wear breathable, natural fabrics; change out of sweaty clothing promptly; shave or trim underarm hair, which can reduce bacterial buildup and odor
When to See a Doctor: Sweating is excessive, sudden in onset, one-sided, or disrupts daily life, which may need medical evaluation

Aliases/Keywords: hives, welts, itchy raised bumps
Common Causes: Allergic reaction, heat, stress, pressure on the skin, sometimes unknown triggers
Natural/Home Remedies: An anti-itch lotion or a colloidal oatmeal bath soak; a cool, damp washcloth applied for 10-20 minutes
Self-Care Tips: Avoid scratching, which can trigger more hives; keep fingernails short and clean; wear loose clothing
When to See a Doctor: Hives come with swelling of the lips/tongue/throat, difficulty breathing, or dizziness — this is an emergency; also see a doctor if hives last more than a few days

Issue: Itchy skin from mild eczema flare (self-care only)
Aliases/Keywords: eczema itch, atopic dermatitis itch, dry itchy patches
Common Causes: A flare of a known dry-skin tendency, often triggered by dry air, irritants, or stress
Natural/Home Remedies: Colloidal oatmeal bath soak followed by moisturizer applied to slightly damp skin within a few minutes ('soak and seal'); cool compress for acute itching
Self-Care Tips: Moisturize at least twice daily even between flares; identify and avoid personal triggers (certain fabrics, soaps, stress); keep baths lukewarm and brief
When to See a Doctor: The flare is widespread, weeping, crusted with yellow scale, or not improving with consistent home care — this needs a diagnosis and treatment plan, not just self-care

Aliases/Keywords: red face, flushed cheeks, facial redness
Common Causes: Heat, spicy food, alcohol, sun exposure, skincare irritation, exercise
Natural/Home Remedies: A cool compress to calm sudden flushing; simplifying skincare to fragrance-free, gentle products
Self-Care Tips: Identify and moderate personal triggers (heat, spicy food, alcohol); use a mineral sunscreen; avoid harsh scrubs or hot water on the face
When to See a Doctor: Redness is persistent, comes with visible blood vessels, bumps, or eye irritation — this pattern should be evaluated by a dermatologist rather than self-treated indefinitely

Aliases/Keywords: cellulite, dimpled skin, orange-peel skin texture
Common Causes: Fat distribution beneath the skin interacting with connective tissue bands; very common and normal
Natural/Home Remedies: Regular moisturizing can improve how skin looks and feels, though it does not remove the underlying texture
Self-Care Tips: Staying active and hydrated supports overall skin health; this is a normal variation in skin, not a medical problem
When to See a Doctor: N/A — this is a cosmetic variation, not a medical concern, so there is no medical red flag to watch for

Aliases/Keywords: dull skin, lackluster skin, tired complexion
Common Causes: Dead skin cell buildup, dehydration, lack of sleep, poor circulation
Natural/Home Remedies: Gentle exfoliation once or twice weekly; a hydrating serum or moisturizer with humectant ingredients
Self-Care Tips: Stay hydrated; prioritize sleep; a short daily walk can improve circulation and complexion over time
When to See a Doctor: N/A for dullness alone, but mention any accompanying fatigue, weight change, or other symptoms to a doctor

Aliases/Keywords: diaper rash, nappy rash, incontinence-associated rash
Common Causes: Prolonged contact with moisture, urine, or stool against the skin
Natural/Home Remedies: Gentle cleansing with plain water or a mild, fragrance-free cleanser; a barrier ointment (e.g. zinc oxide or petroleum jelly) applied after cleaning
Self-Care Tips: Change soiled clothing/pads promptly; let the skin air-dry fully before applying a barrier product; avoid scented wipes
When to See a Doctor: The rash has open sores, bleeding, or looks infected (pus, spreading redness, fever)

Issue: General skincare / how to build a simple routine
Aliases/Keywords: skincare routine, basic skincare, skin care steps
Common Causes: N/A — general prevention and maintenance question
Natural/Home Remedies: A simple daily routine: gentle cleanser, fragrance-free moisturizer, and broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+) every morning
Self-Care Tips: Introduce new products one at a time; avoid over-exfoliating; check your skin regularly for any new or changing spots
When to See a Doctor: You notice a new mole or spot that is asymmetric, has an irregular border, uneven color, is larger than a pencil eraser, or is changing — get this checked promptly
